# Value Contracts

These shared types describe values used by plot attributes and mark channels.
The TypeScript types are exported by `@uwdata/mosaic-spec`. JavaScript uses
native values and the existing vgplot runtime; Python authoring uses its own
host adapters. JSON/YAML specifications contain serializable values.

The owning value definition and the complete specification can admit different
values. Existing attribute unions also include parameter-reference strings;
the generated contracts preserve their current admission behavior. For example,
the ColorScheme definition accepts canonical scheme names and objects, while
the complete plot attribute union also admits lowercase and uppercase strings.
Use the documented canonical values in portable specifications.

`Fixed` is the string `"Fixed"` in a declarative specification. JavaScript
uses the existing `vg.Fixed` Symbol. The parser supplies that Symbol to the
runtime; generating declarations does not create a replacement identity.

## Host applicability

| Native host value | Adapter |
| --- | --- |
| `vg.Fixed` | The declarative Fixed string resolves through PlotFixedNode to the existing vg.Fixed Symbol. |
| `Date` | Native JavaScript Date values use the TypeScript `Interval<Date>` branch. Date parameters cross JSON/YAML as `{date: ISO string}` definitions; the retained parser constructs Date values. |
| `CSSStyleDeclaration` | TypeScript adapts the DOM CSSStyleDeclaration interface through Partial and Omit. Wire values use CSS string properties plus numeric length; native style objects pass through the existing attribute setter. |
| `Function` | JavaScript callback values stay in the existing mark and attribute runtime. JSON/YAML and native wire admission have no callback representation, and Python value aliases exclude callables. |

## CSSStyles

CSS style properties for a plot. TypeScript adapts CSSStyleDeclaration; the wire contract admits string properties and a numeric length.
TypeScript adapts `CSSStyleDeclaration` with these omitted members: `parentRule`, `getPropertyPriority`, `getPropertyValue`, `item`, `removeProperty`, `setProperty`. The wire contract has 534 named string properties for editor completion, numeric `length`, and permits additional string-valued keys.

## Fixed

A symbol indicating a fixed scale domain. A fixed domain is initially determined from data as usual, but subsequently "fixed" so that it does not change over subsequent interactive filtering, ensring stable comparisons.
Starter: [YAML](/templates/values/fixed.yaml), [JSON](/templates/values/fixed.json), [JavaScript](/templates/values/fixed.js), <a :href="withBase('/templates/values/fixed.py')" download>Python</a>.

## LiteralTimeInterval

A named, plural, or numeric time interval string. TypeScript constrains its template forms; the current wire definition admits any string.
The dotX starters use a named parameter because the current mark runtime
interprets a bare interval string as a column name. Passing the interval
through a parameter keeps it constant: JSON/YAML use `$interval`, JavaScript
uses `Param.value(...)`, and Python uses `param(...)`.

The TypeScript numeric time template is projected as an unrestricted string in the existing wire schema. This preserves admission; it does not imply that arbitrary interval strings have runtime implementations.

## TimeIntervalName

The built-in time intervals; UTC or local time, depending on context. The
*week* interval is an alias for *sunday*. The *quarter* interval is every three months, and the *half* interval is every six months, aligned at the start of the year.
Values: `"second"`, `"minute"`, `"hour"`, `"day"`, `"week"`, `"month"`, `"quarter"`, `"half"`, `"year"`, `"monday"`, `"tuesday"`, `"wednesday"`, `"thursday"`, `"friday"`, `"saturday"`, `"sunday"`.

The dotX starters use a named parameter because the current mark runtime
interprets a bare interval string as a column name. Passing the interval
through a parameter keeps it constant: JSON/YAML use `$interval`, JavaScript
uses `Param.value(...)`, and Python uses `param(...)`.

## Interval

How to partition a continuous range into discrete intervals; one of:

- a named time interval such as *day* (for date intervals)
- a number (for number intervals), defining intervals at integer multiples of *n*
TypeScript selects the date or numeric interval branch from its generic argument. The existing wire-schema projection selects the default's first branch; it accepts time-interval strings and rejects numeric values at the Interval definition. The [numeric interval starter](/templates/values/numeric-interval.js) demonstrates `Interval<number>` in JavaScript. It is a native JavaScript example; the wire definition has no matching numeric variant.

The dotX starters use a named parameter because the current mark runtime
interprets a bare interval string as a column name. Passing the interval
through a parameter keeps it constant: JSON/YAML use `$interval`, JavaScript
uses `Param.value(...)`, and Python uses `param(...)`.

## ScaleName

The built-in scale names; one of:

- *x* - horizontal position
- *y* - vertical position
- *fx* - horizontal facet position
- *fy* - vertical facet position
- *r* - radius (for dots and point geos)
- *color* - color
- *opacity* - opacity
- *symbol* - categorical symbol (for dots)
- *length* - length (for vectors)

Position scales may have associated axes. Color, opacity, and symbol scales may have an associated legend.
Values: `"x"`, `"y"`, `"fx"`, `"fy"`, `"r"`, `"color"`, `"opacity"`, `"symbol"`, `"length"`.

## PositionScaleType

The supported scale types for *x* and *y* position encodings.

For quantitative data, one of:

- *linear* (default) - linear transform (translate and scale)
- *pow* - power (exponential) transform
- *sqrt* - square-root transform; *pow* with *exponent* = 0.5
- *log* - logarithmic transform
- *symlog* - bi-symmetric logarithmic transform per Webber et al.

For temporal data, one of:

- *utc* (default, recommended) - UTC time
- *time* - local time

For ordinal data, one of:

- *point* (for position only) - divide a continuous range into discrete points
- *band* (for position only) - divide a continuous range into discrete points

Other scale types:

- *identity* - do not transform values when encoding
Values: `"linear"`, `"pow"`, `"sqrt"`, `"log"`, `"symlog"`, `"utc"`, `"time"`, `"point"`, `"band"`, `"threshold"`, `"quantile"`, `"quantize"`, `"identity"`.

## ColorScaleType

The supported scale types for *color* encodings.

For quantitative data, one of:

- *linear* (default) - linear transform (translate and scale)
- *pow* - power (exponential) transform
- *sqrt* - square-root transform; *pow* with *exponent* = 0.5
- *log* - logarithmic transform
- *symlog* - bi-symmetric logarithmic transform per Webber et al.

For temporal data, one of:

- *utc* (default, recommended) - UTC time
- *time* - local time

For ordinal data, one of:

- *ordinal* - from discrete inputs to discrete outputs

For color, one of:

- *categorical* - equivalent to *ordinal*; defaults to *observable10*
- *sequential* - equivalent to *linear*; defaults to *turbo*
- *cyclical* - equivalent to *linear*; defaults to *rainbow*
- *threshold* - encodes using discrete thresholds; defaults to *rdylbu*
- *quantile* - encodes using quantile thresholds; defaults to *rdylbu*
- *quantize* - uniformly quantizes a continuous domain; defaults to *rdylbu*
- *diverging* - *linear*, but with a pivot; defaults to *rdbu*
- *diverging-log* - *log*, but with a pivot; defaults to *rdbu*
- *diverging-pow* - *pow*, but with a pivot; defaults to *rdbu*
- *diverging-sqrt* - *sqrt*, but with a pivot; defaults to *rdbu*
- *diverging-symlog* - *symlog*, but with a pivot; defaults to *rdbu*

Other scale types:

- *identity* - do not transform values when encoding
Values: `"linear"`, `"pow"`, `"sqrt"`, `"log"`, `"symlog"`, `"utc"`, `"time"`, `"point"`, `"band"`, `"ordinal"`, `"sequential"`, `"cyclical"`, `"diverging"`, `"diverging-log"`, `"diverging-pow"`, `"diverging-sqrt"`, `"diverging-symlog"`, `"categorical"`, `"threshold"`, `"quantile"`, `"quantize"`, `"identity"`.

## ContinuousScaleType

The supported scale types for continuous encoding channels.

For quantitative data, one of:

- *linear* (default) - linear transform (translate and scale)
- *pow* - power (exponential) transform
- *sqrt* - square-root transform; *pow* with *exponent* = 0.5
- *log* - logarithmic transform
- *symlog* - bi-symmetric logarithmic transform per Webber et al.

For temporal data, one of:

- *utc* (default, recommended) - UTC time
- *time* - local time

Other scale types:

- *identity* - do not transform values when encoding
Values: `"linear"`, `"pow"`, `"sqrt"`, `"log"`, `"symlog"`, `"utc"`, `"time"`, `"identity"`.

## DiscreteScaleType

The supported scale types for discrete encoding channels. One of:

- *ordinal* - from discrete inputs to discrete outputs
- *identity* - do not transform values when encoding
Values: `"ordinal"`, `"identity"`.

## ProjectionName

The built-in projection implementations; one of:

- *albers-usa* - a U.S.-centric composite projection with insets for Alaska and Hawaii
- *albers* - a U.S.-centric *conic-equal-area* projection
- *azimuthal-equal-area* - the azimuthal equal-area projection
- *azimuthal-equidistant* - the azimuthal equidistant projection
- *conic-conformal* - the conic conformal projection
- *conic-equal-area* - the conic equal-area projection
- *conic-equidistant* - the conic equidistant projection
- *equal-earth* - the Equal Earth projection Šavrič et al., 2018
- *equirectangular* - the equirectangular (plate carrée) projection
- *gnomonic* - the gnomonic projection
- *identity* - the identity projection
- *reflect-y* - the identity projection, but flipping *y*
- *mercator* - the spherical Mercator projection
- *orthographic* - the orthographic projection
- *stereographic* - the stereographic projection
- *transverse-mercator* - the transverse spherical Mercator projection
Values: `"albers-usa"`, `"albers"`, `"azimuthal-equal-area"`, `"azimuthal-equidistant"`, `"conic-conformal"`, `"conic-equal-area"`, `"conic-equidistant"`, `"equal-earth"`, `"equirectangular"`, `"gnomonic"`, `"identity"`, `"reflect-y"`, `"mercator"`, `"orthographic"`, `"stereographic"`, `"transverse-mercator"`.

## Interpolate

How to interpolate range (output) values for continuous scales; one of:

- *number* - linear numeric interpolation
- *rgb* - red, green, blue (sRGB)
- *hsl* - hue, saturation, lightness (HSL; cylindrical sRGB)
- *hcl* - hue, chroma, perceptual lightness (CIELCh_ab; cylindrical CIELAB)
- *lab* - perceptual lightness and opponent colors (L\*a\*b\*, CIELAB)
Values: `"number"`, `"rgb"`, `"hsl"`, `"hcl"`, `"lab"`.

## SymbolType

The built-in symbol implementations. For fill, one of:

- *circle* - a circle
- *cross* - a Greek cross with arms of equal length
- *diamond* - a rhombus
- *square* - a square
- *star* - a pentagonal star (pentagram)
- *triangle* - an up-pointing triangle
- *wye* - a Y with arms of equal length

For stroke (based on [Heman Robinson’s research][symbol-research]), one of:

- *circle* - a circle
- *plus* - a plus sign
- *times* - an X with arms of equal length
- *triangle2* - an (alternate) up-pointing triangle
- *asterisk* - an asterisk
- *square2* - a (alternate) square
- *diamond2* - a rotated square

The *hexagon* symbol is also supported.

[symbol-research]: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10618600.2019.1637746
Values: `"asterisk"`, `"circle"`, `"cross"`, `"diamond"`, `"diamond2"`, `"hexagon"`, `"plus"`, `"square"`, `"square2"`, `"star"`, `"times"`, `"triangle"`, `"triangle2"`, `"wye"`.

## FrameAnchor

How to anchor a mark relative to the plot’s frame; one of:

- *middle* - centered in the middle
- in the middle of one of the edges: *top*, *right*, *bottom*, *left*
- in one of the corners: *top-left*, *top-right*, *bottom-right*, *bottom-left*
Values: `"middle"`, `"top-left"`, `"top"`, `"top-right"`, `"right"`, `"bottom-right"`, `"bottom"`, `"bottom-left"`, `"left"`.

## ReducerPercentile

A percentile reducer from p00 through p99, with common percentile names retained as TypeScript completion hints.
## Reducer

How to reduce aggregated (binned or grouped) values; one of:

- *first* - the first value, in input order
- *last* - the last value, in input order
- *count* - the number of elements (frequency)
- *distinct* - the number of distinct values
- *sum* - the sum of values
- *proportion* - the sum proportional to the overall total (weighted frequency)
- *proportion-facet* - the sum proportional to the facet total
- *deviation* - the standard deviation
- *min* - the minimum value
- *min-index* - the zero-based index of the minimum value
- *max* - the maximum value
- *max-index* - the zero-based index of the maximum value
- *mean* - the mean value (average)
- *median* - the median value
- *variance* - the variance per [Welford’s algorithm][welford]
- *mode* - the value with the most occurrences
- *pXX* - the percentile value, where XX is a number in [00,99]
- *identity* - the array of values

[welford]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_calculating_variance#Welford's_online_algorithm

## Python host values

These aliases live in `vgplot._types` for binding annotations. They describe
Python host values rather than adding callable public constructors. Python
runtime serialization, caller discovery, and object identities are retained.
An omitted mark channel uses the existing `UNSET` singleton; explicit `None`
remains distinct. Callback functions are outside these Python value aliases.

### ChannelValue

Values for mark channels, including native dates and parameter objects.

```python
ChannelValue = (
    str | float | bool | date | dict[str, Any] | Sequence[Any] | _ParamBase | None
)
```

### AttrValue

Values for plot attributes, preserving explicit None and native date objects.

```python
AttrValue = (
    str | float | bool | date | dict[str, Any] | Sequence[Any] | _ParamBase | None
)
```

### MarkData

Named sources, source helpers, native frames, or inline values used as mark data.

```python
MarkData = (
    str
    | FromRef
    | DataDef
    | IntoFrame
    | dict[str, Any]
    | Sequence[Any]
    | _ParamBase
    | None
)
```

### TransformArg

Scalar, expression, or parameter arguments accepted by Python transform helpers.

```python
TransformArg = str | float | bool | dict[str, Any] | _ParamBase
```

### MimeBundle

A display MIME mapping, an accompanying metadata pair, or no bundle.

```python
MimeBundle = dict[str, str] | tuple[dict[str, Any], dict[str, Any]] | None
```


| Host adapter | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `date` | Dates stay native in channels and attributes; date parameters serialize as ISO date values. |
| `IntoFrame` | Native dataframes remain host objects and use caller variable names as table references. |
| `_ParamBase` | Runtime parameter objects resolve to named references through object identity. |
| `DataDef/FromRef` | Data definitions and source helpers retain their runtime classes and resolve named data references. |
| `UNSET` | The existing vgplot._types sentinel stays a singleton; omitted channels remain distinct from explicit None. |
| `unsupported` | Python value aliases exclude callback objects; native JavaScript callbacks use their separate target adapter. |

The <a :href="withBase('/templates/values/python-adapters.py')" download>Python host-adapter starter</a>
uses native dates, a dataframe, source references, and the omission sentinel.
It is Python-only; native frame and sentinel objects have no JSON/YAML value representation.
This optional example requires PyArrow (`uv add pyarrow`) alongside vgplot.
